1.0.s.en: 1. The source of wisdom and its characteristics

1.0.0.en: 1 All wisdom is from the Lord, and is with Him for ever. 2 Who can number the sand of the sea, and the drops of rain, and the days of eternity? And who can measure the height of heaven, and the breadth of the earth, and the deep? 3 And who can search out wisdom, which is before all things? 4 Wisdom was created before all things, and the understanding of prudence from everlasting. 5 The fountain of wisdom is the word of God in the highest, and her ways are everlasting commandments. 6 To whom has the root of wisdom been revealed, and who has known her subtlety? 7 To whom has the knowledge of wisdom been made manifest, and who has understood her great experience? 8 There is One who is wise, greatly to be feared, sitting upon His throne. 9 The Lord Himself possessed her, and saw her, and numbered her, 10 and poured her out upon all His works; she is with all flesh according to His gift, and He has given her to those who love Him.

1.0.1.en: All wisdom is from the Lord, and is with Him for ever. [1]

1.0.2.en: True wisdom is from the Lord [1]; He gives it to those who seek it, and it never departs from Him; it is the Son, the Word (1 Cor 1:24). The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of wisdom (Isa 11:2); whoever has the Spirit dwelling in him has wisdom (2 Tim 1:7).

1.0.3.en: When the Lord entered into dialogue with Job, He revealed to him his need of divine wisdom. Job expected God to ask him about certain sins he had committed, and did not expect Him to ask him about matters concerning the wonders of creation, which God made for the sake of every man, and whose secrets man cannot fully know (Job 38). In this God exposed Job's ignorance of how the earth was created (Job 38:4-7), his ignorance of the setting of bounds for the seas (8-11), and of how the light of dawn appears (12-15), and of perceiving the shadow of death and the darkness (16-21), and the clouds, the hail and the thunder... (22-30), the stars and their effect on the earth (31-33), the power of God in the air and in natural phenomena (34-38), and God's care for the irrational animals (39-41).

1.0.4.en: v Our divine Teacher is to be trusted, for He is marked by three wonderful characteristics: prudence, goodness and authority.

1.1.0.en: As for prudence, we say that He is the wisdom of God the Father. "All wisdom is from the Lord, and is with Him for ever." As for authority, we say that He is God the Creator. "All things were made by Him; and without Him was not any thing made that was made" (Jn 1:3). As for His good will, He alone gave Himself as a sacrifice for us. "The good shepherd giveth His life for the sheep" (Jn 10:11). Truly He gave Himself. What is good will but the desire for good for the benefit of one's neighbor? [3]

1.1.1.en: St. Clement of Alexandria The theme of the whole book is the believer's enjoyment of heavenly wisdom. The book begins with the expression "all wisdom," as though the book wishes to affirm that there are different kinds of wisdom, and that the source of all of them is the Lord.

1.1.2.en: A. Natural wisdom, which the Book of Ben Sirach says is created with the faithful in the womb (Sir 1:12). This wisdom, which believers value as a divine gift, God offers to all humanity without partiality to believer or unbeliever, giving it to each as is fitting. The believer receives it from the hand of God, and so continually offers a sacrifice of thanksgiving in a spirit of humility. The unbeliever boasts of it as a quality peculiar to himself and to no one else, so the ego swells in him, and he falls into arrogance and pride. Many express this by saying that every man admires his own mind, and is neither pleased nor satisfied with what he has of possessions, as though he were marked by pride together with greed.

1.1.3.en: Natural wisdom is characterized by the following: 1. It is a divine gift, yet it is affected by the lives of the parents and their possibilities, abilities and gifts, so the factor of heredity cannot be ignored. 2. What occupies God's mind is not the quantity of the fruits of this wisdom, but the degree of man's faithfulness in what has been given to him of wisdom and its capacities. A person may be crowned with glory even though, by our human judgment, he does not enjoy exceptional brilliance like others. 3. It is fitting for us to respect and appreciate the variety of these abilities: parents may excel in medicine and gain renown for it, while their son feels that his gift lies in industrial, commercial or administrative work, or skill in one of the arts, or exceptional ability in learning new languages.

1.1.4.en: The beauty of the family and of society, as of the Church, lies in the variety of gifts, so that each person feels his need of his brother, and that his success rests on his appreciation of the gifts of his brothers. This variety supports man in humility, as he feels his need of others, and it also helps the spirit of unity and cooperation, so that all work together as a team (team work). 4. This natural wisdom can be developed with a spirit of piety, together with striving and a desire for continual renewal and growth; it can also be allowed to decline until it almost disappears through negligence and failure to kindle the gift.

1.1.5.en: B. The wisdom of study and learning, and also of benefiting from the experience of others and from one's own personal experience in the past. Every man can enjoy this, even if he is an atheist, but the believer realizes that the mind itself is a gift from God, and that all the circumstances surrounding him did not happen haphazardly or by chance, but that the hand of God is at work in all his life, even to the hairs of his head, which are numbered before God. So he is indebted to God for his mind and for his ability to learn and to enjoy the experiences of others and his own experiences.

1.1.6.en: Man enjoys the wisdom of study and learning and the enjoyment of experience without partiality. Truly, by directing natural wisdom toward uprightness, and by not deviating from the free divine gift, we enjoy growth through study and experience. On the contrary, many have buried their natural gifts because of the deviation of their aim and the misconduct of their behavior.

1.1.7.en: C. Heavenly wisdom: It pleases God our heavenly Father that every believer bear the icon of the only-begotten Son, "the wisdom of God" (1 Cor 1:24), which the believer treasures through his enjoyment of the grace of sonship. This wisdom is peculiar to the believer who cleaves to God, for he is united with the wisdom of God, or the Word of God incarnate, and so bears heavenly wisdom. The Apostle James says: "If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him" (Jas 1:5). It is written in the song of wisdom sung by righteous Job:

1.1.8.en: "But where shall wisdom be found? and where is the place of understanding?

1.1.9.en: Man knoweth not the price thereof; neither is it found in the land of the living... seeing it is hid from the eyes of all living...

1.1.10.en: God understandeth the way thereof, and He knoweth the place thereof, etc." (Job 28:12-23).

1.1.11.en: St. Augustine sees that the believer seeks wisdom through his realization that he needs union with the Lord Christ Himself, the wisdom of God. So instead of being confined to himself, man enjoys fellowship with the wisdom of God.

1.2.0.en: v Truly in these books which they study with zeal they read: "For the Lord giveth wisdom: out of His mouth cometh knowledge and understanding" (Prov 2:6). They receive from Him that zeal for study, if it is granted with godliness [4].

1.3.0.en: v Unless a man comes out of himself, he will not become wise, but through God he acquires wisdom [5].

1.4.0.en: St. Augustine v He (Christ) is called Wisdom, as Solomon says... and He is also called "the Firstborn," for the Apostle Paul says of Him: "the firstborn of every creature" (Col 1:15). The Firstborn, then, by nature is not different from Wisdom, but is the very same. Finally the Apostle Paul says: "Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God" (1 Cor 1:24) [6].

1.4.1.en: v There is with God an understanding that you cannot find anywhere except in Christ Jesus. For all the divine attributes are represented in the Lord Christ: He is the wisdom of God; the power of God; the righteousness of God; holiness; and He is salvation; and the understanding of God. Although He is one with the Father in essence, He bears many names that refer to different things. For you do not grasp the same meaning concerning the Lord Christ when you look at Him as Wisdom and when you look at Him as Righteousness.

1.4.2.en: When you look at Him as Wisdom you understand from that His knowledge of divine and human things.

1.4.3.en: And when you look at Him as Righteousness you understand from that His ability to give everyone his due.

1.4.4.en: If you look at Him as Holiness you understand His ability to sanctify all who believe in Him and are consecrated to Him.

1.4.5.en: And you will also perceive Him as Understanding, for He knows good and evil and what is neither good nor evil.

1.4.6.en: Origen Who can number the sand of the sea, and the drops of rain, and the days of eternity? [2]

1.4.7.en: After the wise man calls us to cleave to the Lord so as to enjoy His wisdom, he asks us to touch this surpassing divine wisdom through creation itself, which God brought into being to serve man. He alone numbers the sand of the sea, the drops of rain and all time.

1.4.8.en: Who can search out the height of heaven, and the breadth of the earth, and the depth of the deep (the seas), and wisdom? [3]

1.4.9.en: The wisdom of God is surpassing, and His knowledge is beyond all limits, for He numbers the sand of the sea, the drops of rain, and the days of eternity. Nothing is hidden from Him, for He knows the dimensions of heaven, the size of the earth, and the depths of the seas.

1.4.10.en: Wisdom was created before all things, and prudent understanding from everlasting [4].

1.4.11.en: Some see that the created wisdom given to man is the light that God created on the first day (Gen 1:3). God gave us the light of wisdom so that we may walk as ambassadors for Him in wisdom, discernment, understanding and prudence.

1.4.12.en: And some scholars see that this text concerns the wisdom of God who became incarnate in the fullness of time, although the plan of the Incarnation was in the mind of God before the creation of all things. The incarnate wisdom of God came to save mankind so that they might enjoy the freedom of the glory of the children of God (Rom 8:21-23; Eph 1:10; Col 1:15-17).

1.4.13.en: As for his saying "from everlasting," it shows that the wisdom of God is eternal, without beginning.

1.4.14.en: The wise man links the wisdom created before all things, which He gave to the heavenly beings and to men, with prudent understanding, for it is the eternal hypostasis of Wisdom. Holy Scripture has affirmed that Jesus Christ, the incarnate Word of God, is the wisdom of God the Father (1 Cor 1:24), one with the Father in the same essence.

1.4.15.en: St. Augustine emphasized the distinction between the wisdom of God the Creator and wisdom as a divine gift.

1.4.16.en: v Wisdom was created before all things, and it is certainly not the wisdom that is co-partner and equal to You, O our God, its Father, and by whom all things were made (Jn 1:3), and in whom, as the Beginning, heaven and earth were created (Gen 1:1)... This is called wisdom although it is created. Just as the Light (God) who illumines is different in power from the light which is illumined.

1.5.0.en: How great is the difference between the wisdom that creates and that which is created! It is a great difference, like the difference between the righteousness that justifies and the righteousness that is accomplished by justification? [7]

1.5.1.en: v As God it was said: "Before all the hills He begat me" (Prov 8:25), that is, before all the exceedingly great creatures. "Before the morning star I begat You" (Ps 109:3) LXX; that is, before all ages and temporal things. And as the servant it was said: "The Lord possessed me in the beginning of His way" (Prov 8:22).

1.5.2.en: As God He said: "I am the truth," and as the servant: "I am the way."

1.6.0.en: For since He is the firstborn of those who have fallen asleep (Rev 1:5), He prepared the way for His Church to the Kingdom of God and to eternal life; this is the Head who grants immortality to the body. Thus He created in the beginning of the ways of God for His works (or His dispensation) [8].

1.7.0.en: St. Augustine Fulgentius, a disciple of St. Augustine, sees that the wisdom which was created before all things is the wisdom that God gave to the angels when He created them [9].

1.7.1.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa sees that the word "created me" here concerns the humanity, not the divinity.

1.8.0.en: v The expression "created me" refers not to His divinity (and simple nature), but He says so since He assumed our created nature by His divine plan [10].

1.8.1.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa Heavenly wisdom is distinguished by giving the believer a life of fellowship with God, so that he tastes the Fatherhood of the Father and responds to the sweetness of His care under all circumstances, and experiences the salvation of the incarnate Word of God, and rejoices as he sings: "I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me" (Gal 2:20). And he touches the work of the Holy Spirit, who renews and sanctifies him who has enjoyed the new birth in the waters of Baptism, and he experiences the new mercies of God every morning.

1.8.2.en: By the work of the Holy Trinity the believer is prepared for eternal life with the earnest of heaven (Eph 1:14), and as the Apostle says: "he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting" (Gal 6:8).

1.8.3.en: To whom was the root of wisdom revealed?

1.8.4.en: And who has known her wise counsel? [5]

1.8.5.en: Through fellowship with God, the believer enjoys intimate friendship with Him, and the Lord reveals to him the secrets of His wisdom, and gives him knowledge and understanding; he discovers God's wise plan in his own life as well as concerning mankind.

1.8.6.en: There is One who is wise and greatly to be feared, and He sits upon His throne [6].

1.8.7.en: Who is this One who is wise, sitting upon the throne, but the Lord of glory, of whom the Apostle says: "But unto them which are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God" (1 Cor 1:24).

1.9.0.en: v He who truly believes is fully united with Him in whom are truth, divinity, essence, life and wisdom, and sees in Him all these, which are not in him who does not believe. For without the Son of God you would have neither existence nor name, and the strong man becomes without strength, and the wise man without wisdom. For Christ is "the power of God, and the wisdom of God" (1 Cor 24:1), so whoever thinks that he sees the one God without power, truth, wisdom, life or true light, either sees nothing at all or surely sees what is evil [11].

1.9.1.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa The Lord is He who created her, and saw her, and numbered her, and poured her out upon all His works [7].

1.9.2.en: Here he speaks of the wise plan of God concerning His rational creation in heaven and on earth.

1.9.3.en: God poured out wisdom upon all His works, meaning that the Father created all things by the Son, the Word. As the Evangelist says: "All things were made by Him" (Jn 1:3).

1.9.4.en: She is with all flesh (man) according to His gift, and He gave her (abundantly) to those who love Him [8].

1.9.5.en: Ben Sirach says that wisdom dwells with every man (believer) according to what is given to him, and God gives it to those who love Him. This gift is not static, but ever-growing (dynamic). He who fears the Lord grows in wisdom and increases in it, as it is said in the Book of Proverbs: "A wise man will hear, and will increase learning; and a man of understanding shall attain unto wise counsels" (Prov 1:5).

1.9.6.en: The Lord gives man His blessings and distributes them according to man's needs and abilities, and also according to his love and the breadth of his heart. If God offers everything, even wisdom, by a certain measure, then on our part it is fitting for us in every work to walk with wisdom, balance and moderation, without exaggeration on the right or on the left.

1.10.0.en: v He who receives the teachings of wisdom in addition to the first teachings, since he is already wise, receives the following teachings in matters in which he was not previously wise, and so becomes wiser. As it is also said: "When the wise man hears these things, he becomes wiser" [12].

1.11.0.en: Origen v This is the duty of those who are zealous for the good pleasure of God, that they ask what is best for them to do [13].

1.12.s.en: 2. Wisdom and the fear of the Lord

1.12.0.en: 11 The fear of the Lord is glory, and boasting, and gladness, and a crown of rejoicing. 12 The fear of the Lord delights the heart, and gives gladness and joy and length of days. 13 He who fears the Lord will be well at the last, and will find favor in the day of his death. 14 The love of the Lord is glorious wisdom. 15 And those to whom she appears love her when they see her and contemplate her wonders. 16 The beginning of wisdom is the fear of God. She was created with the faithful in the womb, and has made her nest among men for ever, and will entrust herself to their seed. 17 The fear of the Lord is the worship of Him with knowledge. 18 Worship keeps the heart and justifies it, and gives gladness and joy. 19 He who fears the Lord will be well, and will find favor in the day of his death. 20 The fullness of wisdom is the fear of the Lord; she makes men drunk with her fruits. 21 She fills all her house with desirable things, and her storehouses with grain. 22 The crown of wisdom is the fear of the Lord; she makes peace and healing and health to flourish, 23 and she saw wisdom and numbered it, and both are a gift from God. 24 Wisdom pours out knowledge and the understanding of prudence, and exalts the glory of those who possess her. 25 The root of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, and her branches are length of days. 26 In the treasures of wisdom are understanding and worship with knowledge, but to sinners wisdom is an abomination. 27 The fear of the Lord drives away sin. 28 The wrath of the wicked cannot be justified, for the burden of his wrath makes him fall. 29 He that is longsuffering will endure for a time, and afterward joy will return to him. 30 The sensible man hides his words for a time, and the lips of the faithful will praise his understanding.

1.12.1.en: The book made clear that the beginning of the enjoyment of wisdom is the acquisition of the fear of the Lord, by which the believer is prepared to receive wisdom as a divine gift. The fear of the Lord is not unjust, but leads to honor; indeed it is a crown of glory, exaltation, happiness and constant rejoicing for man even to the moments of death. Ben Sirach distinguishes between the fear that causes shame and disgrace, and the fear that gives honor and glory (4:20-21) together with constant joy. The first fear afflicts man like a psychological illness, driving him into a state of frustration, and the holy fear, which he distinguishes by the title "the fear of the Lord," is a good gift that God gives to His children.

1.12.2.en: The fear of the Lord is glory and boasting and gladness and a crown of rejoicing [9].

1.12.3.en: The fear of the Lord is the source of the believer's delight and joy [11-13]. The fear of the Lord is the feeling of honoring Him with deep spiritual thought, together with walking in the Spirit of the Lord in moderation and propriety. The blessings of holy fear are:

1.12.4.en: A. It is a boast, in which the believer glories as he shares with the heavenly beings who praise God in the spirit of glorious holy fear [9].

1.12.5.en: B. It gladdens the heart with a joy that time cannot shatter [10].

1.12.6.en: C. It kindles the heart with longing for the last day of the Lord, so the believer does not fear death [11].

1.13.0.en: D. This fear can be granted to the children of believers while they are in the womb, as happened with John the Baptist (Lk 1:44), and Jacob the son of Isaac (Rom 9:11-13), and Samuel the son of Hannah [12].

1.14.0.en: E. Heavenly wisdom gives inward satisfaction, and gives health to the soul as a medicine for it [16].

1.14.1.en: F. He who fears the Lord is kept from falling into sins and evil thoughts that seem natural, over which man has no authority.

1.14.2.en: The link between wisdom and the fear of the Lord lies in the fact that the wisdom books are in essence a call to cleave to the Lord Christ, the wisdom of God, and to enjoy His icon through the daily work of the Holy Spirit in us, so that we enjoy the constant divine presence in our life. This divine presence moves us to the fear of the Lord, so that we are made worthy, more and more, of an abundance of divine work in us.

1.14.3.en: v Where God is, there is the fear of the Lord, there is gentle seriousness, watchful care and eager concern for others, testing with good examination, fellowship that has its weight, fitting progress, obedience with piety, service with a spirit of consecration, unaffected appearance, a renewed church life, and everything that is divine [14].

1.14.4.en: Tertullian v Question: Why is there sometimes a kind of sorrow of heart and contrition in the fear of the Lord that comes upon the soul without great effort, and happens spontaneously, and at other times there is in the soul a kind of dullness, so that even if a man forces himself, he cannot feel any contrition of heart?

1.14.5.en: Answer: Such contrition is a gift from God, for He stirs up the desire, and the soul tastes the sweetness of such contrition that is stirred up, and so adopts it (adopts the grace given to it). Or it is to prove that the soul is able, through intense zeal, to be in continual contrition. Thus he who loses this grace through his laxity has no excuse.

1.14.6.en: But sometimes we force ourselves (to contrition), yet we are unable to obtain it, as evidence of our earlier neglect on other occasions. For it is impossible for man to succeed in a work merely by coming to it without giving it intense care together with diligent training with others, and his soul is shown to be disgusted with the vices and passions that hinder the practice of what is fitting. This is according to the teaching spoken by the Apostle, who said: "But I am carnal, sold under sin. For that which I do I allow not: for what I would, that do I not; but what I hate, that do I" (Rom 7:14-15). He also says: "Now then it is no more I that do it, but sin that dwelleth in me" (Rom 7:17).

1.14.7.en: God allows this very thing to happen to us for a good purpose, that the soul, by means of the things it suffers involuntarily, may perceive the things that assail it, and as it learns the ways by which it became enslaved to sin against its will (Rom 6:20), it awakens again, and guards itself against the snares of the devil (1 Tim 3:7; 6:9), and discovers that God's mercy urges the support of those who truly repent [15].

1.14.8.en: v For my sake You turned my mourning into joy for me, You tore my sackcloth, and girded me with gladness" (Ps 30:12).

1.14.9.en: The joy of God does not settle in all souls, but in those souls which wept over their sins with continual tears, like one who has lost someone dear to them. God turns the mourning of such a soul into joy, and sorrow is profitable here...

1.14.10.en: The prophets weep over us, and call us to weep until we discover our faults in the light of their prophetic words; then we weep over our perdition, and subdue our body with striving and discipline.

1.14.11.en: The man who walks in such a way, his sackcloth is torn, and he puts on the adorned wedding garment so as not to be cast outside the wedding (Mt 22:11-13) [16].

1.14.12.en: St. Basil the Great Thus the book transfers us from dry rational wisdom to the holy practical wisdom set forth in Holy Scripture. It is not fearful cowering, but godliness, consecration to God and glorying in Him (Prov 2:1-5). The believer does not separate divine love from the fear of the Lord (Deut 10:12; Sir 2:15). The fear of the Lord is not foreign to the believer; it is granted to him while he is still a fetus in the womb [12].

1.14.13.en: The fullness of wisdom is the fear of the Lord [16]. It makes believers drunk with its delightful fruits, and satisfies their souls with its choice food, and fills their storehouses with its produce, and gives them inward peace and perfect health.

1.14.14.en: The fear of the Lord is not only the beginning of wisdom, but its fullness and its crown. By the fear of the Lord the believer receives the abundant harvest of wisdom. Among the blessings of the fear of the Lord is that it drives away sins, and removes all anger from the soul, for "the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God" (Prov 15:18; Jas 1:20).

1.14.15.en: Thus the book links wisdom, the divine commandment and the fear of the Lord. At the same time it warns against wavering between pagan Hellenistic ideas and faithfulness in fellowship with God.

1.14.16.en: v In any case, it is beneficial to fear Him alone, not as one who is unjust but as God who is righteous. For a man fears one who is unjust lest he destroy him by injustice, and fears the righteous one lest he sin and be punished.

1.15.0.en: By your fear of Him you are freed from all harmful fears. For unless you fear the one Lord, the Creator of all, you become a slave to all the evils that harm you, I mean you become a slave to demons and (spiritual) diseases and everything that can harm you in one way or another [17].

1.15.1.en: v Fear God, for He is just, but whether you fear Him or love Him you must not sin...

1.16.0.en: He who fears Him can gain victory over evil desires, and does not covet what belongs to others, but practices tenderness and dignity and works justly! [18]

1.16.1.en: The Clementines By the fear of the Lord we enjoy the blessed life; St. Arsenius says that he who fears the One (God) will not fear many.

1.16.2.en: v As a lamp lights a dark room, so the fear of the Lord, when it penetrates the heart of a man, illumines it, teaching it all the virtues and the commandments of God.

1.17.0.en: One of the Desert Fathers v Blessed is he who walks in all things in fear through reverent modesty. For he stands firm in the truth, able to say: "I advanced and saw the Lord before me at all times, for He is at my right hand, that I should not be moved" (Ps 16:8) [19] LXX.

1.18.0.en: St. Basil the Great St. Barsanuphius gives us a practical training for obtaining the crown of rejoicing, for he wrote: [Labor with all your strength, and then God will help you by the prayers of your fathers. For He thirsts for your salvation, since He swore by Himself that He does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he return and live" (Ezek 18:23)... Contribute like the widow with the two mites that you have, and He will be pleased as He was with her (Mk 12:42). Hasten with your boat to the ship of your fathers, and they will lead you to Jesus, who alone can give you humility, strength, prudence and the crown of rejoicing [20].]

1.19.0.en: v Rejoice in the Lord, rejoice in the Lord, rejoice in the Lord. May the Lord guard your soul and body and spirit from all evil, and from every opposition of the devil, and from all wearisome imaginings. May the Lord be your light and your protection and your way and your strength and the crown of your rejoicing and your everlasting support. Take heed to yourself, as it is written: "even the word that is gone out of my lips shall not be changed" (Ps 89:34) [21]

1.19.1.en: St. Barsanuphius The Lord's word in the Book of Malachi concerning the men of the priesthood shows His divine work in their lives, for He fills them with fear as an ornament with which the priests are adorned, so that they enjoy glory and rejoicing, and are adorned with holiness.

1.19.2.en: v "I do this so that he (the priest) may be filled with fear toward Me; I work in such a way that he trembles before My name" (Mal 2:5) LXX. He counts in a fitting manner all the exalted adornment of the priesthood, which he obtains through the teaching of the Law. He inspires first and before everything the fear of the Lord in the service of divine worship, making them drawn to tremble before His name with fear and trembling when they hear the name of the Lord, and brings them into the experience of inclining toward reverence (of the Lord), not as a matter of no importance, but with seriousness, for there is nothing more important than it... It was said: "The fear of the Lord is glory and boasting." Thus he secures safety for him who practices the priesthood with holiness and in truth.

1.20.0.en: He did not ask them merely to be refreshed by fear, but to be completely filled with fear, that is, that the fear of the Lord fill all the heart and the soul [22].

1.21.0.en: v Consider how God uses a means fitting to Him: instead of punishing us, He displays the effects of His wrath on human bodies, preferring to alarm us with simple outward terrors and slight losses [23].

1.22.0.en: St. Cyril the Great v The starting point in the service of God [as slaves] is being filled with the spirit of fear, when the person is still called a child. For children in particular, fear is the tutor. Therefore the Apostle says of such a child: "Now I say, That the heir, as long as he is a child, differeth nothing from a servant, though he be lord of all; but is under tutors and governors until the time appointed of the father. Even so we, when we were children, were in bondage under the elements of the world" (Gal 4:1-3) [24].

1.22.1.en: Origen St. Ambrose, in his discourse on Cain and Abel, compares what the world offers with what the Church offers. The world is unable to give the soul true pleasure and inward joy, whereas the Church, where the wisdom of God and the fear of the Lord are, makes the soul drunk with the joy of the Spirit, together with wisdom and prudence from God.

1.23.0.en: v "Come, eat of my bread, and drink of the wine which I have mingled" (Prov 9:6). Do you find delight in songs that enchant listeners at banquets? Listen to the voice of the Church, which urges us not only in the Song of Songs: "Eat, O friends; drink, yea, drink abundantly, O beloved" (Song 5:1), but this drunkenness makes men sober. This drunkenness is grace (from God) and not madness of the mind [25].

1.23.1.en: St. Ambrose The fear of the Lord gladdens the heart, and gives gladness and joy and length of days [10].

1.23.2.en: The blessings of the fear of God extend in the life of man in this world to the moment of his death, when he meets the Lord Christ face to face.

1.23.3.en: v If anyone wishes to obtain the love of God, let the fear of the Lord be in him, for fear begets weeping, and weeping begets strength. And when all these are perfected in the soul, the soul begins to bear fruit in everything. And when God sees in the soul these good fruits, He smells them as the fragrance of sweet incense, and He and His angels rejoice in it, and He satisfies it with joy, and keeps it in all its ways until it reaches its place of rest without suffering harm.

1.23.4.en: When Satan sees the great heavenly Guardian surrounding the soul, he fears to approach it or attack it because of this great power.

1.23.5.en: Therefore acquire this power so that the demons may be terrified before you, and your works become easy, and you may delight in the divine work, for the sweetness of the love of God is sweeter than honey.

1.23.6.en: Truly many monks and virgins in the communities have not tasted this divine sweetness, and have not acquired the divine power, supposing that they have obtained it, although they have not striven. But he who strives for it obtains it surely through the divine mercies, for God is no respecter of persons.

1.23.7.en: So he who wants to have the light of God and His power must despise the honors of this world and its defilement, and hate all the things of the world and the pleasure of the flesh, and cleanse his heart from all evil thoughts. And he offers to God fasts and tears night and day without relenting as pure prayers; then God pours out upon him that power.

1.24.0.en: Strive to obtain this power, so that you may do all your works with ease, and have great boldness before God, and He will give you all that you ask [26].

1.24.1.en: St. Anba Anthony the Great He who fears the Lord, it shall go well with him at the last, and in the day of his death he shall be blessed [11].

1.24.2.en: When we speak of Jacob's ladder, by which Jacob enjoyed the opened heaven and fellowship with the heavenly beings, we recall that Jacob suffered from fear. He was in complete isolation, with no father or mother or brother or friend to accompany and support him. He was on his way, fleeing from the violence of his brother, suffering many dangers and an unknown future. Jacob leaned on the stone, a type of the Lord Christ, to sleep, and he enjoyed the heavenly vision, and touched the fear of the Lord, for he said: "How dreadful is this place! this is none other but the house of God" (Gen 28:17).

1.24.3.en: When we suffer from the fear of the flesh or the fear of the world that crushes the soul, we lean on our Christ, the cornerstone, and He replaces destructive fear with holy fear. Instead of our fear of the world with all its harsh circumstances, we see the glory of God and His holiness and His love, so we look forward with joy to the day of our departure from the world, and we realize that while we are on earth we dwell in the house of God, indeed we have become "of the household of God" (Eph 2:19); how much more blessed then will be the day of our death.

1.24.4.en: The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord; it is created with the faithful in the womb [12].

1.24.5.en: God's care for man goes back to the moment of the beginning of his conception, and continues while the fetus is in his mother's womb. The Lord Christ showed His concern for the faith of infants and children (Lk 18:15-17).

1.24.6.en: St. Philoxenus distinguishes between different kinds of fear: the fear of slaves, the fear of hired servants, the fear of friends, and the fear of sons.

1.24.7.en: v There is one who fears being beaten, and this is the fear of slaves; and there is one who fears losing his wages, and this is the fear of hired servants; and there is one who fears being deprived of the inheritance, and this is the fear of sons; so although fear has only one name, the differences among its kinds are many.

1.24.8.en: The holy prophets feared God, and the Jewish people also from time to time feared God; but how great is the difference between the two fears!

1.25.0.en: For the prophets feared to grieve God as His friends, because they loved Him; while the Jews feared His discipline and punishment as slaves [27].

1.25.1.en: St. Mar Philoxenus Our Christ wants to raise us by His grace until we reach the fear of sons. So we do not fear God as slaves who fear their master, carrying out the commandment not from their depths but for fear of punishment.

1.25.2.en: Nor do we fear Him as hired servants who fulfill the commandment for the sake of the wages or for fear of being deprived of them; thus God would be a means and not an end, and we would submit to Him to obtain His blessings and not to possess Him and enjoy fellowship with Him.

1.25.3.en: Nor do we fear Him as mere friends who seek to please their friend.

1.25.4.en: But we fear Him as sons, fulfilling the commandment so that the image of our Father may be formed in our depths, and so we are prepared for fellowship in His glories. We possess Him and He possesses us, and we live with Him eternally in His embrace!

1.25.5.en: St. Augustine sees that the way begins with fear and raises man up the ladder of holiness until he reaches wisdom: "The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord."

1.26.0.en: v The prophet Isaiah presents to us the seven well-known spiritual gifts. He begins with wisdom and ends with the fear of the Lord, as though he were descending from the heights to our own level. He does this to teach us to climb up again. Thus he begins from where we want to arrive (wisdom), and comes to the point of beginning. He says: "The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and godliness, the spirit of the fear of the Lord" (Isa 11:2). So he descended from wisdom to fear, not to slip backward, but to teach us to climb from fear and ascend to wisdom. We do this so that we may advance, "for the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom [28]."

1.27.0.en: St. Augustine v It is fitting for the souls of those who wish to speak wisdom first to be purified by the divine fear. For distributing the sacraments of salvation to the common people and receiving all persons on an equal footing (without wise discernment), including those whose lives are not adorned with purity, and who have not been tested nor prepared to use the sacraments reasonably, is like pouring precious ointment into a filthy vessel [29].

1.28.0.en: St. Basil the Great v Just as among the pagans there are those who abstain from the pleasures before them, either because it is impossible to obtain what they see, or for fear of men, or to obtain greater pleasures, so also with regard to the faith, some practice self-control, either because they await the promise of God or for the fear of the Lord; such self-control rests on knowledge and on the enjoyment of better things, and is counted as striving for perfection. It is said: "The fear of the Lord is the head of wisdom" (Prov 1:7) [30].

1.28.1.en: St. Clement of Alexandria v The beginning of wisdom is fear, for it is fitting that we not begin with (spiritual) contemplations and leave fear. For unrestrained contemplation may drive us to the edge of a precipice. Rather we must be broken and purified, so that through fear we become light in weight, and rise to the heights.

1.29.0.en: For where there is fear there is keeping of the commandments, and where there is keeping of the commandments there is purification of the flesh from the cloud that covers the soul and does not allow it to see the divine ray. And where there is purification there is illumination, and illumination is the satisfaction of the desires of those longing for great things, or for things that surpass all great things [31].

1.29.1.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus v Let us not allow the beast (sin) to be unbridled; let us hasten to it and put a strong muzzle on every side, which is the fear of the coming judgment.

1.30.0.en: When a friend or one of your household causes you to stumble and you become angry, consider that your disobedience is against God, and that the kindness you show to those who trouble you will be repaid to you at your judgment by God's kindness to you [32].

1.30.1.en: St. John Chrysostom She made a foundation for life among men, and continues to be trustworthy with their descendants [13].

1.30.2.en: The blessings of the fear of the Lord are: 1. "It makes men drunk with its fruits" [14], so he who fears the Lord does not feel a hunger for the glory of the world and its desires and treasures, but feels satisfied, for his depths are filled with the fruit of the fear of the Lord. 2. "It fills all their houses with desirable things" [15]. For the fear of the Lord brings him into the divine embrace, and he discovers that His mouth is most sweet and He is altogether desirable (Song 5:16). 3. It fills "their storehouses with its produce" [15]; the rich fool wanted to build larger storehouses and fill them with good things so as to eat and be satisfied, but his soul was required of him that very night before he moved to build the storehouses (Lk 12:20); but he who fears the Lord, the Spirit of God raises up from his depths a dwelling for God the Father and His only-begotten Son, and his depths become a kingdom of God (Lk 17:21), so what does he lack? There dwells in him the Lord of glory, in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom (Col 2:3). 4. The one who fears the Lord is crowned with the crown of wisdom [16], so peace increases in him without ceasing, and he experiences healing, so no sin wounds him, and no wicked thought steals into his mind! 5. God is pleased with the one who fears the Lord, so He numbers what he has enjoyed, and rains upon him the waters of knowledge, learning and practical wisdom (prudence), and raises him from glory to glory [17]. 6. The one who fears the Lord will not fear the departure of wisdom from him, for the fear of the Lord is the root of wisdom and its roots planted in him, and its branches will never wither [20].

1.30.3.en: The delight of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, and it makes men drunk with its fruits [14].

1.30.4.en: St. Wissa, disciple of Anba Shenouda, the Archimandrite, sees that wisdom works not only in the life of the wise man but also in the lives of those around him, and on the contrary folly destroys the man and those who deal with him.

1.31.0.en: v "Every wise woman buildeth her house: but the foolish plucketh it down with her hands" (Prov 14:1). This means that the wise woman encourages her neighbor in the fear of God and with the love in her heart toward her sister and sisters. On the other hand the foolish woman pulls down with her hands, by her words full of bitterness and hatred and contempt. As it is written: "In the mouth of the foolish is a rod of contempt" (cf. Prov 14:3) [33].

1.32.0.en: St. Wissa v It is altogether unfitting that the beatitudes begin from another source (other than poverty in spirit and the fear of the Lord), where the summit of wisdom is attained, for the crown (beginning) of wisdom is the fear of the Lord (1:16), and on the other hand pride is described as the beginning of every sin (10:13). Let the proud man strive for the kingdoms of the earth and love them; but "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven" [34].

1.33.0.en: v For him who strives for wisdom, there is nothing like the saying: "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom" [35].

1.33.1.en: v Listen to Holy Scripture: "The crown (beginning) of wisdom is the fear of the Lord" (Sir 1:16). Therefore he begins with the fear of the day of judgment: by fear he reforms himself, to strive against his enemies, that is, against his sins. Let him begin to renew his life inwardly, and mortify his members which are upon the earth, as the Apostle says: "Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth... (Col 3:5).

1.33.2.en: He calls the spiritual matters of evil "members upon the earth," for he continues explaining this: "covetousness, uncleanness," and so on. So that man who begins with the fear of the day of judgment to mortify his members which are upon the earth extends to the height of his heavenly members and their strengthening. He practices goodness with his heavenly members. And as the heavenly members are raised, longing begins toward the fear. He fears that Christ may come upon this wicked man who wishes to curse him... Now the pure soul which desires to embrace her Bridegroom, and renounces the adulterer, begins to long for the coming of Christ.

1.34.0.en: She becomes a virgin in her depths through this faith and hope and love. Thus the soul has confidence in the day of judgment, and does not resist itself when it prays: "Thy kingdom come" (Mt 6:10). For he who fears the coming of the kingdom of God may be seized by fears lest his prayer be answered [36].

1.34.1.en: St. Augustine She fills all their houses with desirable things, and their storehouses with her produce [15].

1.34.2.en: The crown of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, which gives peace and healing for flourishing [16].

1.34.3.en: The Lord saw her and numbered her, and rained down the power of understanding, and honors the glory of those who hold fast to her [17].

1.34.4.en: The root of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, and its branches are length of days [18][37].

1.34.5.en: The fear of the Lord is the steering wheel of the soul; the Holy Spirit of God gives it to us, He who alone is able to bring us from glory to glory, and to give us grace upon grace, through our fellowship with the Lord of glory, the holy Jesus. The fear of the Lord brings us into the royal way, so we do not swerve toward sin, nor toward self-righteousness. It keeps us from the blows from the left and from the right, until we enter into the bosom of the holy heavenly Father.

1.34.6.en: v The fear of the Lord urges the soul to keep the commandments, and through keeping the commandments the house of the soul is built.

1.34.7.en: v Let us fear the Lord and build houses for ourselves, so that we may find shelter in the winter where there is rain and thunder, for he who has no house suffers great dangers in the time of winter.
